title: Official business
title_target: Em muốn thuê phòng hai đêm ạ.
goal: Handle things at a guesthouse, a post office and a bank — and ask for help in three different polite ways.
bekal: renting a room, filling in a form, and asking about checkout time
asking with *giúp em*, *cho em* and *làm ơn*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Nhận phòng khách sạn
dialogs.intro: A small guesthouse in Huế. Budi turns up without a booking, and it's the first time he's handled everything by himself in Vietnamese.

lines.speaker: Lễ tân:
lines.text: Chào anh, anh cần gì ạ?
lines.id: Hello, how can I help you?
lines.baca: Chào ang, ang kần gì ạ?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Em muốn thuê phòng hai đêm ạ.
lines.id: I'd like to rent a room for two nights.
lines.literal: younger-sibling want rent room two night (polite).
lines.baca: Em muốn thuê fòng hai dêm ạ.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Chưa ạ. Còn phòng không chị?
lines.id: No. Do you still have rooms?
lines.baca: Chưa ạ. Kòn fòng không chị?

lines.speaker: Lễ tân:
lines.text: Còn ạ. Anh cho em xem hộ chiếu nhé.
lines.id: We do. May I see your passport?
lines.literal: still (polite). older-brother let younger-sibling see passport OK.
lines.baca: Kòn ạ. Ang cho em sem hộ chiếu nyé.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Đây ạ. Một đêm bao nhiêu tiền ạ?
lines.id: Here it is. How much per night?
lines.baca: Dây ạ. Một dêm bao nyiêu tiền ạ?

lines.speaker: Lễ tân:
lines.text: Bốn trăm nghìn một đêm, đã bao gồm ăn sáng.
lines.id: Four hundred thousand a night, breakfast included.
lines.literal: four hundred thousand one night, already include eat morning.
lines.baca: Bốn chăm ngìn một dêm, dã bao gồm ăn sáng.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Phòng có wifi và điều hoà không ạ?
lines.id: Does the room have Wi-Fi and air conditioning?
lines.baca: Fòng kó wifi và diều hoà không ạ?

lines.speaker: Lễ tân:
lines.text: Có đầy đủ ạ. Anh điền vào tờ khai này giúp em.
lines.id: Everything. Please fill in this form.
lines.literal: have complete (polite). older-brother fill into sheet declaration this help younger-sibling.
lines.baca: Kó dầy dủ ạ. Ang diền vào tờ khai này zúp em.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vâng. Mấy giờ phải trả phòng ạ?
lines.id: OK. What time do I have to check out?
lines.literal: yes. how-many hour must return room (polite)?
lines.baca: Vâng. Mấy zờ fải chả fòng ạ?

lines.speaker: Lễ tân:
lines.text: Mười hai giờ trưa ạ. Chúc anh ở vui vẻ!
lines.literal: twelve hour noon (polite). wish older-brother stay happy!
lines.baca: Mười hai zờ chưa ạ. Chúk ang ở vui vẻ!

notes: ⚠️ **Staff call themselves *em* and call you *anh*, whatever their age.** In service jobs — receptionists, shop assistants, waiters — the person serving almost always picks pronouns that place the guest above them. Don't be confused if a fifty-year-old woman calls herself *em* with you; it's the courtesy of the job, not of age.

**Cho em xem literally means "let me see", and it's the politest way to ask to look at something.** Its cousins are *cho em hỏi* ("may I ask"), *cho em mượn* ("may I borrow"). The pattern *cho + person + verb* is one of the ones you'll need most after *cho tôi* in unit 4.

**Giúp em at the end of a sentence means "for me, please"** — you saw it in unit 9. Notice that here it's the **receptionist** asking: *Anh điền vào tờ khai này giúp em.* The form works both ways, and it's much softer than a bare command.

**Đã bao gồm means "already included"**, a phrase you must recognize in anything you pay for: *đã bao gồm ăn sáng* (breakfast included), *đã bao gồm thuế* (tax included). The question: *Có bao gồm … không ạ?*

**Nhận phòng and trả phòng are "check in" and "check out"** — literally "receive the room" and "return the room". Vietnamese translates foreign terms far more often than it borrows them, and the results are usually guessable once you know the basic words.

**Điền vào means "fill in" for forms.** *Vào* after it means "into" — you saw direction words attached to verbs in unit 13. *Tờ khai* is a form to fill in; *tờ* is the classifier for sheets, from unit 4.

grammars.title: Three ways to ask politely
body: All three are polite, but they feel different and sit in different places. Choose according to what you're asking for.
after: ⚠️ **Làm ơn sounds more distant and formal than beginners expect.** It's not a "please" to sprinkle everywhere; in casual conversation it actually feels stiff. For everyday matters, *giúp em* and *được không ạ?* are much warmer and far more common.

Adding *nhé* at the end of a request makes it softest: *Gọi taxi giúp em nhé.* Adding *ạ* makes it most respectful: *Cho em hỏi một chút ạ.* Two little words from unit 17, put to really important work.

grammars.title: Documents and luggage
body: You'll be asked for these at guesthouses, airports and government offices. Learn to recognize the written forms, since you'll often read them before you hear them.
after: ⚠️ *Giấy* means "paper", and almost every document name uses it as its head: *giấy tờ* (papers), *giấy phép* (permit), *giấy khám sức khoẻ* (health certificate). Once you recognize *giấy*, you can tell something is a document before you know which one.
*Ký* means "sign" and *ký tên* means "sign your name": *Anh ký vào đây giúp em.* — "please sign here". You'll hear that sentence at every counter.

English
rows: Em muốn gửi thư về Indonesia.
Em muốn gửi thư về Indonesia.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *Gửi* means "send" **and** "leave in someone's care": *gửi thư* (send a letter), *gửi xe* (leave your motorbike at a parking lot). You'll need the second one a lot — almost every building in Vietnam has a *nhà gửi xe*, and you must keep the ticket.
*Cho em xin …* is the politest way to ask for small things: *Cho em xin hoá đơn.* (may I have the receipt), *Cho em xin thêm đá.* (could I have more ice). It sounds much softer than plain *cho em*.

Tôi không nói dượk tiếng Việt nyiều.

blocks.title: Three things to sort out before you go
items: **Keep a copy of your passport separate from the passport itself.** Guesthouses usually ask for the original at *nhận phòng* and return it right away; if someone holds on to it longer, the sentence is *Cho em xin lại hộ chiếu ạ.*
**Vietnam's emergency numbers:** 113 police (*công an*), 114 fire department, 115 ambulance. Keep your embassy's number in Hà Nội in two places — on your phone and on paper.

**Cash is still king outside the big cities.** Street stalls, markets and street-corner motorbike taxis are almost all *tiền mặt*. The sentence you need: *Ở đây có nhận thẻ không ạ?* — and be ready for a "no".
I'd like to rent a room for two nights.
What time do I have to check out?

exercises.prompt: What do you say in each situation? One Vietnamese sentence.
items: You've lost your wallet at the market.
You want to know whether the shop takes cards.
You want to exchange money at the bank.
You want to ask whether anyone speaks English.
